behavior_items: The primary template `template <auto... Methods> struct Foo;` declares a class template whose non-type template parameter pack uses C++17 `auto` deduction. Each element of `Methods...` may have its type deduced independently from the supplied value, so the instantiation site `Foo<&Bar::baz>` asks the compiler to deduce the non-type argument as a pointer-to-member-function value.

The partial specialization attempts to match that deduced non-type pack against a more structured pattern: `template <typename Class, typename... ReturnType, ReturnType (Class::*...Methods)()> struct Foo<Methods...>`. This means GCC must determine whether the incoming `auto` non-type arguments can be interpreted as a pack of member function pointers of the form `ReturnType (Class::*)()`.

The pattern is unusual because it combines three pack-related mechanisms at once: an `auto` non-type parameter pack in the primary template, a non-type parameter pack of member-function pointers in the specialization, and a type parameter pack `typename... ReturnType` that is used as the return type component of each member-function-pointer declarator. The compiler therefore has to perform partial-specialization matching and deduction across both type packs and non-type packs simultaneously.

For the concrete argument `&Bar::baz`, the referenced member is a non-static member function `int Bar::baz()`. Therefore the natural successful match is `Class = Bar`, `Methods... = { &Bar::baz }`, and the return-type portion corresponding to that single method is `int`. Clang accepts this interpretation and compiles the code, showing that the source is intended to be valid template matching rather than inherently ill-formed code.

Once the specialization is selected, `Foo<&Bar::baz>` becomes an empty class type whose only relevant member is `constexpr void operator()() { }`. The body of that call operator does nothing, so at runtime `Foo<&Bar::baz>{}();` should simply construct a temporary empty object and invoke a no-op member function.

The reproducer exercises not only template argument deduction but also code generation for a specialization reached through that deduction. GCC does not fail during parsing or ordinary semantic diagnosis; instead, it accepts the template structure far enough to instantiate and proceed toward generating code for `tryOut()`.

The reported failure occurs "during RTL pass: expand", which is a late backend/code-generation stage. That is significant because the source-level construct is purely template metaprogramming plus a trivial function call, so a backend crash strongly suggests that earlier C++ front-end processing produced an invalid or inconsistent internal representation for the instantiated specialization or its call operator.

The crash point at `Foo<&Bar::baz>{}();` indicates that the trigger is actual use of the instantiated specialization, not merely its declaration. The compiler likely delays some work until the object construction or operator-call expression forces full instantiation and lowering of the selected specialization.

A particularly stress-inducing aspect of the example is the declarator `ReturnType (Class::*...Methods)()`, where the pack expansion applies to member-function-pointer names while the return-type component is written as a separate template parameter pack. Even with only one method in the pack, GCC has to associate the deduced class type, function type, and value argument coherently. The ICE implies that this association is mishandled internally in GCC 9.x.

The code contains no overload set, cv-qualification, ref-qualification, or argument list complexity; `Bar::baz` is a simple zero-argument non-const member returning `int`. This minimality is useful because it isolates the bug to the interaction of partial specialization and auto-deduced member-function-pointer non-type arguments, rather than any complicated callable semantics.

Because the operator body is trivial and the class has no data members, there is no legitimate reason for code generation to need complex runtime logic. A conforming compiler should either reject the program with a proper front-end diagnostic if it considered the specialization invalid, or, as Clang does, compile it quietly. A segmentation fault is therefore definitive evidence of a compiler bug rather than user-code undefined behavior.

The reproducer demonstrates that GCC 9.2.x mishandles a valid-or-at-least-front-end-accepted template specialization pattern involving deduced non-type template parameter packs of member function pointers. The internal compiler error is backend-visible, but the root cause is most plausibly an incorrect front-end representation created during partial-specialization matching and instantiation.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer defines a primary template parameterized by an `auto...` non-type pack and a partial specialization that matches that pack as zero-argument member function pointers. Instantiating `Foo<&Bar::baz>` should deduce a single element corresponding to `int (Bar::*)()`, select the specialization, and call a trivial no-op `operator()`. Clang compiles this successfully. GCC 9.2 accepts the code far enough to instantiate it, but then crashes with an internal compiler error during the RTL `expand` phase when compiling `Foo<&Bar::baz>{}();`. This shows the bug is triggered by GCC's handling of partial specialization/deduction for auto-deduced member-function-pointer non-type template parameter packs, producing invalid internal state that later causes a segmentation fault in code generation.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is an interaction bug between three C++17 template features: an `auto...` non-type template parameter pack in the primary template, partial specialization that reinterprets that pack as member-function-pointer NTTPs, and simultaneous deduction of associated type information (`Class` and return type components) from those values. The program is minimal and semantically simple: a single zero-argument non-const member function `int Bar::baz()`, a selected specialization, and a trivial empty `operator()`. GCC accepts the construct through parsing, template matching, and instantiation, but crashes only when the instantiated specialization is actually used and lowered for code generation. Because the ICE appears in RTL expand rather than during template diagnostics, the strongest pattern is that the C++ front end likely builds an inconsistent or malformed internal tree/type representation for the specialized `Foo<&Bar::baz>` or its call expression, which later backend expansion assumes is valid and dereferences unsafely. The defect is therefore most plausibly in GCC's handling of partial-specialization deduction and canonicalization of auto-deduced pointer-to-member-function NTTP packs, with the backend crash being a downstream symptom of corrupted front-end state.
possible_causes: Incorrect C++ front-end deduction logic for partial specializations matching `auto...` NTTP packs against pointer-to-member-function parameter packs, especially when deriving both the class type and function return type from the NTTP value.

Malformed internal representation of the deduced member-function-pointer type/value for `&Bar::baz` after specialization selection, such as constructing an invalid `TREE_TYPE`/function type for the NTTP pack element.

Bug in pack substitution/canonicalization when a non-type pack expansion (`...Methods`) is tied to separately deduced type parameters, causing mismatched pack lengths or an invalid association between `ReturnType`, `Class`, and `Methods`.

Failure in instantiation of the selected class specialization or its `operator()`, where GCC carries an incomplete or null type for the specialized class because the partial-specialization match involving member-function-pointer NTTPs was not fully normalized.

Backend expand assuming a valid front-end object/function expression for `Foo<&Bar::baz>{}();` and crashing because the front end emitted a broken constructor/call tree for a class reached through this unusual NTTP specialization path.

Missing validation or ICE guard in cp/pt code for C++17 `auto` non-type template arguments that are pointer-to-member functions, allowing invalid internal state to propagate into RTL generation instead of being rejected or diagnosed earlier.

Incorrect handling of zero-argument member function pointer signatures in template argument substitution for partial specializations, specifically around representing `ReturnType (Class::*)()` as a deduced pattern from an `auto` NTTP.

Defect in template specialization matching for pointer-to-member-function constants where the value argument is accepted but not fully converted/canonicalized to the specialization's expected NTTP type before later code generation uses it.
evidence: The failure is triggered by `template <auto... Methods>` combined with a partial specialization `ReturnType (Class::*...Methods)()`, which points directly to GCC logic for matching auto-deduced NTTP packs to structured pointer-to-member-function patterns.

The concrete argument `&Bar::baz` is minimal: a single non-static member function with signature `int Bar::baz()`, no overloads, cv-qualifiers, parameters, or other complications, narrowing the bug to template/NTTP handling rather than callable semantics.
Clang accepts the code, supporting that the source pattern is intended to be valid and that GCC's crash is not due to an inherent source error.

GCC does not reject the code in parsing or semantic analysis; it proceeds far enough to instantiate and compile `tryOut()`, indicating the bad state is created after or during specialization matching/instantiation rather than lexical parsing.

The ICE occurs during `RTL pass: expand`, a late code-generation phase, which is strong evidence that earlier front-end template processing produced an invalid internal representation later consumed by the backend.
The crash happens specifically at the use site `Foo<&Bar::baz>{}();`, showing that actual instantiation/lowering of the selected specialization and call operator is required to expose the bug.

The selected specialization's `operator()()` is trivial and the class is effectively empty, so there is no legitimate complex backend work here; a segfault implies corrupted compiler IR rather than difficult user-code semantics.

The behavior analysis explicitly highlights that the root cause is most plausibly an incorrect front-end representation created during partial-specialization matching and instantiation, with the backend crash as a downstream symptom.

gcc/cp/call.cc.signature: static tree build_op_delete_call_1 (enum tree_code code, tree addr, tree size, bool global_p, bool coro_p, tree placement, tree alloc_fn, tsubst_flags_t complain)
gcc/cp/call.cc.summary: Build a call to operator delete. This has to be handled very specially, because the restrictions on what signatures match are different from all other call instances. For a normal delete, only a delete taking (void *) or (void *, size_t) is accepted. For a placement delete, only an exact match with the placement new is accepted. CODE is either DELETE_EXPR or VEC_DELETE_EXPR. ADDR is the pointer to be deleted. SIZE is the size of the memory block to be deleted. GLOBAL_P is true if the delete-expression should not consider class-specific delete operators. CORO_P is true if the allocation is for a coroutine, where the two argument usual deallocation should be chosen in preference to the single argument version in a class context. PLACEMENT is the corresponding placement new call, or NULL_TREE. If this call to "operator delete" is being generated as part to deallocate memory allocated via a new-expression (as per [expr.new] which requires that if the initialization throws an exception then we call a deallocation function), then ALLOC_FN is the allocation function.

DIAG_LOCATION is just another DECL. NO_ACCESS_REASON is an optional parameter used to specify why DECL wasn't accessible (e.g. ak_private would be because DECL was private). When we have only some of our vector isa extensions enabled, then there are some modes for which vector_mode_supported_p is false. For these modes, the generic vector support in gcc will choose some non-vector mode in order to implement the type. By computing the natural mode, we'll select the proper ABI location for the operand and not depend on whatever the middle-end decides to do with these vector types. The midde-end can't deal with the vector types > 16 bytes. In this case, we return the original mode and warn ABI change if CUM isn't NULL. Generate insns to zero all st registers together. Return true when zeroing instructions are generated. Assume the number of st registers that are zeroed is num_of_st, we will emit the following sequence to zero them together: fldz; \ fldz; \ ... fldz; \ fstp %%st(0); \ fstp %%st(0); \ ... fstp %%st(0); i.e., num_of_st fldz followed by num_of_st fstp to clear the stack mark stack slots empty. How to compute the num_of_st: There is no direct mapping from stack registers to hard register numbers. If one stack register needs to be cleared, we don't know where in the stack the value remains. So, if any stack register needs to be cleared, the whole stack should be cleared. However, x87 stack registers that hold the return value should be excluded. x87 returns in the top (two for complex values) register, so num_of_st should be 7/6 when x87 returns, otherwise it will be 8. return the value of num_of_st.

The reproducer involves a trivial class call operator and member-function-pointer template specialization, with no vector semantics, so despite its defensive purpose it is very unlikely to be the best fix location.
